extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and representatives who file trademark documents before the USPTO (attorneys, non-patent practitioners, paralegal service managers), USPTO disciplinary stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and sanctions governing electronic signature practices on USPTO trademark filings, supervisory obligations over non-practitioner assistants, and related ethical duties and remedial requirements following impermissible signing.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO electronic signature requirement (37 C.F.R. § 2.193)
rubrics_metrics.description: All electronic signatures must be personally entered by the person named as the signatory on the trademark document; a proper person must sign the trademark document. A person signing electronically must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces and/or punctuation marks adopted as a signature, placed between two forward slash ('/') symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission. See 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a)(2), (c), (e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The electronic signature must be manually entered by the named signatory (keystrokes entered personally). Failure to have the named signatory personally enter the signature (e.g., having a paralegal type the signatory's electronic signature) does not comply with § 2.193 and invalidates the signature for USPTO purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP guidance on electronic signatures (TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: TMEP states: 'All documents must be personally signed. The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory. Just as signing the name of another person on paper does not serve as the signature of the person whose name is written, typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP explicitly forbids a paralegal or assistant from entering the electronic signature of the named signatory. This guidance explains the practical application of the regulation (e.g., use of forward slashes and personal keystroke entry) and treats typing another's signature as not valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must provide competent representation to a client, which includes the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners representing trademark applicants before the USPTO are reasonably expected to be knowledgeable of USPTO regulations and guidance pertaining to electronic signing of USPTO trademark documents; failing to understand applicable signature rules can constitute a violation of § 11.101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner having direct supervisory authority over a non-practitioner assistant must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the non-practitioner's conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable supervision includes ensuring compliance with USPTO signature regulations and TMEP guidance. Allowing or permitting non-practitioner assistants (e.g., VPS paralegals) to personally enter the named signatory's electronic signature rather than ensuring the named signatory personally enters it demonstrates inadequate supervision under § 11.503(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are prohibited from engaging in conduct involving misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing or allowing the filing of documents that contain an electronic signature entered by someone other than the named signatory can amount to misrepresentation under § 11.804(c) because the submission falsely purports to bear the signatory's personal entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are prohibited from engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting non-signatories to enter another person's electronic signature on filings submitted to the USPTO may be prejudicial to the integrity of the trademark registration process and thus violate § 11.804(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep clients reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an ethical obligation to keep clients reasonably informed about the status of matters entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a practitioner learns of an impermissibly signed trademark filing, the practitioner may have an ethical obligation to inform the client of the actual or potential consequences to a pending application or issued registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to inform the USPTO when impermissibly signed documents were filed (37 C.F.R. § 11.303)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an obligation not to make misrepresentations to the USPTO and not to engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the integrity of the USPTO trademark registration process; where a practitioner learns that impermissibly signed documents have been filed, the practitioner may have the ethical obligation to inform the USPTO promptly of the affected trademark filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duty is tied to the general prohibitions on misrepresentation and prejudicial conduct; prompt disclosure to the USPTO may be required upon discovery of improperly signed submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial responsibility for paralegals and non-practitioner assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner with ultimate managerial authority over paralegals and non-practitioner assistants is responsible for ensuring that their conduct is compatible with the practitioner's professional obligations, even if those assistants take directions from or are generally supervised by others (e.g., client practitioners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ultimate managerial authority carries the obligation to implement office policies and supervision practices (e.g., requiring named signatories to enter their own electronic signatures) to prevent impermissible signing; relying solely on client supervision is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner expectation not to file or allow filings that do not comply with USPTO electronic signature rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners representing trademark applicants before the USPTO are reasonably expected not to file, or allow to be filed, declarations or other trademark documents that do not comply with the agency's electronic signature regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expectation reinforces duties under §§ 11.101, 11.504(b), 11.804(c), and 11.804(d); failure to ensure compliance can create ethical and disciplinary exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction: Public reprimand and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: As an agreed-upon sanction, the Respondent shall be publicly reprimanded, and the OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at OED's electronic FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the provided text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Official Gazette notice text describes the violation and the regulatory citations; publication serves both as sanction and public notice of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required client notification (remedial requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 30 days of the Final Order, Respondent must notify in writing (to the direct applicant client or the client practitioner retained by VPS) each of the clients in the 35 affected trademark filings of: (1) the lack of compliance with the USPTO electronic signature regulations; (2) the potential and actual adverse consequences to the applicant's intellectual property rights in the pending application(s) or registered mark(s); and (3) corrective action to be taken, if any, to address the potential and actual adverse consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification must be sent via U.S. Postal Service certified mail, return receipt requested. The Respondent must then submit an affidavit with corroborating evidence that notifications were sent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of notification and corroborating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 45 days of the Final Order approving the settlement, the Respondent shall submit an affidavit to the OED Director stating compliance with the client-notification requirement and provide corroborating evidence (e.g., copies of the written notification and evidence of delivery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a documented compliance checkpoint for the remedial client-notification obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CLE remedial requirements and corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Within six months from the date of the Final Order, the Respondent shall enroll, complete, and receive Continuing Legal Education credit under the rules of the Delaware State Bar for at least two courses totaling four hours where the primary subject matters are (i) law office management and (ii) trademark practice before the USPTO. Within seven months the Respondent must submit an affidavit with copies of certificates of course completion, descriptions of course content, and copies of written materials provided to course participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These requirements are designed to remedy deficiencies in law office management and substantive knowledge regarding trademark practice and signature compliance; documentary proof must be submitted to OED.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of proceeding record for future disciplinary consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the Settlement Agreement prevents the USPTO from considering the record of this disciplinary proceeding, including this Final Order, in: (1) addressing further complaints or evidence of the same or similar misconduct; (2) in any future disciplinary proceeding against the Respondent as an aggravating factor or to rebut statements by or on Respondent's behalf; and (3) in connection with any request for reconsideration under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disciplinary record may be used to enhance sanctions or as evidence in future matters; practitioners should expect long-term consequences from published disciplinary records.
